title: What Is AI?
html:
Artificial Intelligence is the study and construction of agents that act intelligently — systems that perceive their situation, reason about it and choose actions that achieve goals. Machine learning is one (now dominant) way to build them; search, logic and probability are the others.

Artificial Intelligence — the field that builds computer systems able to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence — perceiving, reasoning, planning, learning, understanding language and acting in the world.

Artificial Intelligence
→
Machine Learning
→
Deep Learning
→
Generative AI / LLMs

Every arrow is a subset: all deep learning is machine learning, and all machine learning is AI — but a chess engine using search, a route planner using A* and a medical expert system using rules are AI without any learning. Those classical techniques are what this subject covers; learning-based AI has its own notes (Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Generative AI).

Four ways to define AI

Russell & Norvig's classic textbook sorts definitions along two axes — thinking vs acting, and matching humans vs being rational (doing the right thing):

Human-likeRational
ThinkingThinking humanly — cognitive modelling: build programs that reason the way people do (cognitive science)Thinking rationally — the “laws of thought”: correct inference with formal logic
ActingActing humanly — the Turing test: behave indistinguishably from a personActing rationally — the rational agent: act to achieve the best expected outcome
Key point

Modern AI mostly follows the rational agent approach: it is general (logic is one tool, not the only one), and “best expected outcome” is mathematically precise — unlike “human-like”.

The Turing test and the Chinese room

Turing test (1950)

A human judge chats by text with a hidden person and a hidden machine. If the judge can't reliably tell which is which, the machine passes. Passing needs natural-language processing, knowledge representation, automated reasoning and machine learning. The total Turing test adds computer vision and robotics.

Chinese room (Searle, 1980)

A person who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to answer Chinese notes and looks fluent from outside. Searle's point: manipulating symbols (syntax) is not the same as understanding (semantics) — so passing the Turing test would not prove a machine thinks.

A 1966 program already shows why acting human is a weak test of being intelligent. ELIZA imitated a therapist with a handful of pattern → template rules and no understanding at all:

Weak vs strong, narrow vs general

TermMeaningStatus
Weak AIMachines can act as if they were intelligentPhilosophical claim — widely accepted
Strong AIMachines that act intelligently really think / have mindsPhilosophical claim — open (Chinese room debate)
Narrow AI (ANI)Excels at one task or domain: chess, face recognition, spam filtering, translationEvery deployed system today
General AI (AGI)Human-level competence across essentially all cognitive tasks, able to transfer and learn new onesResearch goal; LLMs are broader than older systems but debated
Superintelligence (ASI)Far exceeds humans in every domainHypothetical — central to AI-safety discussions
Watch out

Don't mix the two pairs up: weak/strong is about whether the machine has a mind; narrow/general is about how many tasks it can do. A system could in principle be general but “weak”.

A short history — booms and winters

YearMilestone
1943McCulloch & Pitts model a neuron as a logic gate
1950Turing, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” — the imitation game
1956Dartmouth workshop (McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, Rochester) — the name “artificial intelligence”; the field is born
1958–66Perceptron (Rosenblatt), Samuel's learning checkers player, the General Problem Solver, LISP, ELIZA
1969–73Minsky & Papert show single perceptrons can't learn XOR; the Lighthill report criticises AI's “combinatorial explosion”
1974–80First AI winter — promises unmet, funding cut
1980–87Expert systems boom (XCON at DEC, MYCIN-style rule bases); Japan's Fifth Generation project; backprop popularised (1986)
1987–93Second AI winter — Lisp-machine market collapses, expert systems prove brittle and costly to maintain
1990s–2000sProbabilistic AI (Bayesian networks, HMMs), statistical ML; Deep Blue beats Kasparov (1997)
2011–12IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!; AlexNet wins ImageNet — the deep-learning era begins
2016AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol — deep networks + Monte Carlo tree search + reinforcement learning
2017–nowThe Transformer (2017), large language models, ChatGPT (2022), multimodal models and LLM agents

Symbolic AI (“GOFAI”)

Knowledge written as symbols and rules; intelligence = search + logical inference. Transparent and precise, but brittle and hand-built. Dominated 1956–1990.

Statistical / connectionist AI

Knowledge learned from data as probabilities or network weights. Robust and scalable, but data-hungry and hard to interpret. Dominant since the 1990s–2010s.

Key point

Winters followed hype: early researchers predicted human-level AI “within a generation”, then hit the combinatorial explosion of search and the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck of hand-written rules. Both problems — and the techniques built to tame them — are the core of this subject.

What is the difference between AI, machine learning and deep learning?

AI is the broad goal of building intelligent agents, by any method — search, logic, probability or learning. Machine learning is the subset where behaviour is learned from data instead of programmed. Deep learning is the subset of ML using many-layered neural networks.

What is the rational agent approach, and why is it preferred?

An agent is rational if, for every percept sequence, it picks the action expected to maximise its performance measure given what it knows. It's preferred because it is well-defined mathematically and general — it doesn't require copying human thought, and logical inference is just one way to act rationally.

What were the AI winters?

Periods of collapsed funding and interest (roughly 1974–80 and 1987–93) that followed over-promising: search didn't scale to real problems (combinatorial explosion) and expert systems were brittle and expensive to maintain.
